paper_title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.

sections.content: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human handobject demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable armhand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clips handobject motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human handobject datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10 faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on real robot. 1. Introduction Dexterous robot policies learn from demonstrations, which are slow and costly to collect by teleoperation [17, 29, 53]. Human handobject interaction, in contrast, is easier to capture [1, 12, 19, 24, 42, 46, 48, 52] and covers more diverse tasks than teleoperation [16, 55]. Many recent methods therefore convert human data into robot data [15, 16, 20, 21, 25, 28, 34, 40, 53, 56]. Kinematic methods map human hand keypoints to robot joint angles by optimization or inverse kinematics (IK) [47, 53]. Physics-based methods search for robot motion that reproduces the object motion in simulation, using sampling-based optimization [34] or reinforcement learning (RL) [21, 28, 56]. Several of these Corresponding author. Figure 1. DexEngine turns human demonstrations into physically executable data for whole bimanual robot, in under 5 GPUminutes per clip. methods build robot datasets this way [16, 21, 34, 53], and UniDex [53] and HuRo [16] pretrain policies on them. Yet these data fall short as training data for whole-robot policies in three ways. First, kinematic methods [16, 53] ignore dynamics: without contact and force, the robot may fail to move the object, and HuRo [16] uses its trajectories as pretraining supervision only. Second, most physicsbased methods [20, 21, 23, 28, 34, 56] ignore the arm: they drive floating hands and leave the arms joint limits, reach, and collisions unchecked, even though policy must control both arm and hand joints. Third, physics-based methods do not scale: the few that include the arm [14, 15, 40] cover fewer than thousand human demonstrations, and most are either slow or inaccurate on many clips. We present DexEngine, scalable pipeline that turns human capture data into physically executable, train-ready simulation data for bimanual robots with dexterous hands. It rests on two key ideas. First, it solves the arms before it searches each clips scene placements for one physics: that the arms can follow, and keeps nearly every clip that has such placement. By contrast, attaching the arms after floating-hand correction keeps 26% fewer clips, even at our placements (Sec. 4.1). Second, it reuses this arm IK solution in residual RL, whose policy acts on the wrist pose in task space and never observes the arm joints. Since IK has mul1 Figure 2. DexEngine pipeline. Human demonstrations are split into clips, scene placement that the arms reach without penetration is found, and the resulting kinematic reference is corrected in physics simulation. The corrected motions become train-ready data for four robot hands, with pose and visual augmentation. Red marks penetration in the kinematic reference, and green the corrected contact. tiple solutions for wrist pose, each random start [36] resets the arm to this solution instead of re-solving IK, which would switch branches and lower accuracy (Tab. 3). With this recipe, even with the arms attached, DexEngine corrects up to 64 clips with one policy, more accurately than existing floating-hand methods, and is the fastest training-based method, at 3.9 GPU-minutes per clip (Tab. 2). Our contributions are fourfold: 1. DexEngine, scalable pipeline that turns human demonstrations into simulation data for whole bimanual robot by solving the arm motion before physics (Sec. 3). 2. An arm attachment for residual RL, acting in wrist space [15] with the arm reset to the kinematic reference at random starts, that keeps the policy accurate and lets it run on rigidly transformed scene without retraining (Tab. 3 and Sec. 3.5). 3. Experiments showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction and mid-training on our data helps at equal fine-tuning budget, also on real robot (Sec. 4). 4. train-ready, physically executable dataset of 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) with contact forces and depth for bimanual robot with each of four dexterous hands, released (Tab. 1). 2. Related work about one billion demonstrations, but only for grasping and opening articulated objects [50]. Human handobject datasets record hand and object trajectories across diverse tasks, without robot actions [1, 12, 19, 24, 42, 46, 48, 52], and HRDexDB [22] adds robot grasps only. Pipelines from human videos reconstruct such trajectories [31] and then retarget them [4, 15, 25, 33, 41, 45], and RoboPaint [11] renders robots retargeted from glove captures into reconstructed scenes. We convert nine human datasets into physically executable armhand trajectories. Human-to-robot retargeting. Retargeting methods differ in whether the robot moves the object as demonstrated. Kinematic retargeting by optimization [47] or IK [53] lets UniDex [53] and HuRo [16] build large robot datasets from human videos, but without contact forces, the robot may fail to move the object. RoboWheel [54] corrects the human handobject poses in physics before retargeting, but not the retargeted robot motion. Physics-based retargeting instead finds robot motion that reproduces the object motion, by sampling-based optimization [34] or RL [21, 28, 41, 56]. To avoid solving each demonstration separately, recent methods fit one model to many [14, 20, 40, 49] or train one to generalize to unseen motions [23]. We correct the retargeted motions with one residual policy per bundle of clips and keep only clips whose objects follow the demonstration. Sources of robot data. Robot training data are teleoperated, synthesized, or converted from human capture. Data generators adapt few teleoperated demonstrations to new scenes [17, 29]. Synthesis without human data reaches Arms and scene placement. An arm-mounted hand can follow demonstration only if its arm can reach every wrist pose without exceeding joint limits or colliding. Floatinghand methods [21, 23, 28] and SPIDERs released data [34] 2 ignore these constraints. EgoEngine [25] mounts the hand on an arm but refines its motion with floating wrist. OATH [40], DexMan [15], and GNR [14] move the arm to follow the retargeted wrist and refine the motion in simulation, but do not search the scene placement, on which IK success depends. Prior pipelines set this placement manually [33], align the robot base kinematically to human videos [16], or pick the candidate base pose with the best IK result [45]. SPIDER [34] samples random placements for single clip and keeps those where IK follows the whole motion. We instead search each clips placements with reachability map [51], as used to place robot bases [27, 44], and run IK only on promising ones before simulation. Policy training on generated and human data. Human and robot data enter three stages of policy training: pretraining, mid-training, and task fine-tuning. UniDex [53], HuRo [16], and PointWAM [35] pretrain on human videos, with or without kinematically retargeted actions, and report gains on fine-tuning. Mid-training adapts the pretrained model to the target robot with robot-matched data [18, 32, 55]. EgoScale [55] and T-Rex [32] report gains from midtraining with teleoperation data, and RLDX-1 [18] adds synthetic episodes from video generative model. In task fine-tuning, most physics-based retargeting methods do not train policies on their output [15, 20, 28, 40, 56] or use it for one to four tasks [21, 25, 34]. EgoEngine [25] finds that executable actions improve policies, but tests this only on single arm. Other methods train RL policies on human data in simulation and run them on real robot directly or via distilled visual policy [6, 7, 9, 13, 26]. We correct wholerobot motions, arms included, across nine human datasets and use the data for both mid-training and task fine-tuning, in simulation and on real bimanual robot. 3. Method 3.1. We train two policies: Diffusion Policy (DP) [8] from scratch and GR00T N1.7 [2] fine-tuned from public weights (Sec. E.9). Results. We test two levels of placement: L0 uses five training placements per clip, and L1 five held-out placements of the same clip. Both hold only scenes where replaying our recorded actions succeeds, and every test scene is thus physically executable. Success requires the object lifted and at its target in P&P, the demonstrated pouring pose in Pour, and tool travel in contact with the target in Sweep (Sec. E.10). Table 4 shows that without physics correction, policies mostly fail: DP succeeds in 0% of rollouts at L0 and 1% at L1, against 53% and 40% on our data. Mid-training and the real robot Mid-training. To use our datas scale and diversity, we mid-train GR00T on all our embodiment-specific data, excluding the source sequences of the task clips, and then fine-tune it as in Sec. 4.2 (Sec. E.9). We deploy GR00T and GR00T + mid on an RB-Y1 with two Wuji 2 hands (row 2 of Fig. 6, right). We test one clip per task, in five trials at fine-tuning placements (L0) and five at held-out ones (L1). Both policies are fine-tuned on these clips from the public and the mid-trained weights, with strong visual augmentation (Sec. E.11). To assess how well the simulated trajectories transfer to the real robot, we also replay each clips recorded trajectory open loop. The replay succeeds in 87% of trials at L0 and 80% at L1 (Tab. 5). The recorded trajectories thus largely transfer to the real robot. GR00T + mid succeeds in 73% at L0 and 27% at L1, against 20% and 0% without it. Mid-training also helps on the real robot, where the policy without it mostly fails. 5. Conclusion We presented DexEngine, data pipeline that turns human handobject demonstrations into physically executable, train-ready data for whole bimanual robot. Searching each clips placement and arm motion before physics keeps the clips the arms can follow. Acting in wrist space and resetting the arm to this motion at random starts let one policy correct up to 64 clips with the arms attached, more accurately than prior floating-hand methods. Policies fine-tuned on kinematic replays of the same clips mostly fail, showing that fine-tuning needs physically accurate handobject interaction. Mid-training on our data helps further, also on real robot. Limitations. Physics correction with closed-loop RL remains costly. Human captures also transfer less often than expected. About third of our clips become robot data  (Fig. 5)  , and Do as Do [33] keeps only 4% of sampled internet videos after reconstruction. Apart from capture defects, most lost clips have no placement the arms can follow from fixed torso and base (Sec. 4.1). Moving the torso and base, or capture guidelines that respect the robots limits, could make more human data usable.

sections.content: This supplement follows the main paper. Sections to detail the four stages of Secs. 3.2 to 3.5. Section gives the setups and further results of Sec. 4, and Sec. shows samples of the recorded data. A. Data preparation details We use the hand poses (MANO [38] parameters), object poses and object meshes of nine public datasets [1, 12, 19, 22, 24, 42, 46, 48, 52]. All sequences are resampled to 50 Hz. A.1. Scene frame, table and supports Frame alignment. Each dataset is converted to z-up frame and rotated about the vertical axis so that the mean direction from the MANO wrist to the fingertips matches that of TACO. HOT3D is aligned per clip instead, since its hand direction varies widely between clips. Table height. The support surface of the main text is the static table on which the objects rest. ARCTIC has none, since its hands often pass below the surface the objects rest on. The sequence defines the table plane in the tabletop datasets (TACO, HO-Cap, DexCanvas, HRDexDB) and in the raw motion-capture frame of OakInk2. For GRAB and H2O, we set the table at the height where objects rest, i.e., stay still for at least 0.5 with no fingertip within 2.5 cm. For HOT3D, we assume the table is the lowest surface on which handled object rests, within the clip or within 2 of it. Handled objects are the manipulated objects and every object that moves in the clip. Supports. An unheld object needs support when it rests at least 1 cm above the table, and whenever it rests in ARCTIC. tracked object directly below it becomes tracked support, which collides with the robot and the objects. Otherwise, disc covering the objects footprint stands under it for the whole clip. Since the real support is not observed and disc can be larger than it, discs collide only with objects and cannot block the robot hand. In the rendered data, each disc stands on pillar down to the table or the floor. manipulates an object. The arm of an inactive hand holds rest pose. When both hands manipulate the same object, it becomes one shared object. A.3. Clip division We take the sequences as the datasets provide them, counting OakInk2 by its annotated primitive tasks (2,828 of the 7,899 sequences of all datasets, Tab. S4). HOT3D sequences are first cut into windows in which hand touches the same object. In every dataset, sequences (for HOT3D, these windows) longer than 15 are split in the middle of an interval in which the objects are still and the hands are away, or otherwise at the slowest wrist motion, so that nearly every piece lasts at least 5 s. Each piece is then cut wherever hand switches to different object on its contact timeline. switch to an object that no hand manipulates counts only if that object moves. Handovers, and alternation between one and two hands holding the same object, stay in one clip. At switch, both clips include the idle gap between the two grasps. A.4. Clip filtering clip is removed when (i) no hand manipulates an object; (ii) tracking fails: in HOT3D, pose gap longer than 0.3 while the object moves; an object that moves by 2 cm or more without contact, fingertip keypoint jump, or an object faster than 3 m/s while the wrist is slow; (iii) the scene is inconsistent, because the object goes more than 2 cm below the table, manipulated object that is not held at the start lies more than 1 cm inside it, the wrist goes more than 5 cm below the table, the estimated GRAB table lies more than 2 cm from the table that GRAB provides, or, in ARCTIC, manipulated object is neither touched by hand nor resting on support; or (iv) the clip is shorter than 1 s. clip is also removed if its retargeted fingertips deviate from the human fingertips by more than 20 mm on average. For the Tesollo and Wuji 2 hands, we remove the hyperextension range, opposite to flexion, of the finger joints from the distal joints up to the MCP joint, since backward-bent fingers give unnatural motion and enlarge the search space of RL. The hand is tilted about its contacting fingertips by at most 20 and lifted by at most 30 mm, keeping the object motion unchanged, and the fingers are then re-solved. Initial hand pose. Of the accepted Wuji 2 clips, 78.0% gained at least one variant trajectory and 65.8% at least three. The duration in Tab. S3 assumes that variant lasts as long as the clips reference. The tables mean lengths exclude the lead-in, while the hours of its clips, trajectories and episodes include it. E. Experiment details E.1. Statistics of the recorded data Table S4 counts, for each robot hand and source dataset, the clips that pass each step of Fig. 5. Recording yields 15,796 Wuji 2 trajectories, 3.13 per accepted clip, with five episodes each. Scored with the metrics of Tab. 2 against their reference object motion, these trajectories reach mean ADD-AUC of 0.935. Of them, 94.2% meet the object criteria of ManipTrans and 95.7% those of SPIDER, and every source dataset reaches an ADD-AUC of at least 0.90. These values describe only the completed rollouts that recording keeps (Sec. D.1) and measure how closely they follow their reference object motion, not how often RL succeeds. The recorded data of the other three hands track as closely. On sample of up to 300 trajectories per hand and source dataset, SharpA, XHand Pro and Tesollo reach ADD-AUC 0.942, 0.937 and 0.933, and the same sampling gives 0.936 for Wuji 2. Their trajectories meet the criteria of ManipTrans in 92.9 to 94.9% and those of SPIDER in 94.8 to 96.4%. ARCTIC clips pass physics correction least often (Tab. S4). Four in five of the ARCTIC clips that the arms can follow turn an articulated part with both hands and without table. Of these, 14 to 26% pass physics correction, against 46 to 62% of its two-hand grasps of whole object. E.2. Conditions of the pipeline comparison DexMan [15], OATH [40] and GNR [14] have no released code, and Tab. 2 does not include them. Clips. The pool holds the 520 of CHORDs released twohanded TACO clips that pass data preparation and kinematic reference generation, in 81 combinations of verb, tool and target. With seed 42 we draw 64 combinations and one clip from each without using any methods ADD-AUC or success rates. The draw skips clips whose motion file CHORDs loader cannot read. Conditions. ManipTrans, DexMachina, SPIDER, EgoEngine and FlashDexRetarget run with our object mass. DexMachina, SPIDER and EgoEngine also use our hand object friction and SharpA finger gains, force limits and armature. CHORD runs as FlashCHORD v0.4, the version of its RL tracker in the code its authors released, and keeps its released assets, including their object mass and inertia. FlashDexRetarget also runs with its support discs switched on, and it trains for 500M environment steps, the end of its default schedule. SPIDER and EgoEngine run in scenes with our table plane, supports (Sec. A.1) and object collision meshes. EgoEngine runs from SPIDERs inputs on the SharpA hand and controls both hands, unlike its TACO setting. EgoEngine runs three times per clip, and we report the mean score over its runs and the time of one run. Cost and training. Costs are GPU-minutes per clip on an NVIDIA L40S. ManipTrans and DexMachina train each clip until its learning curve flattens, for at most 150 minutes. Trained for 200 iterations instead of 1,600, our single-clip policies reach ADD-AUC 0.940, SP-SR 98.4 and MP-SR 85.9 at 43.1 GPU-minutes per clip. This is about third of the GPU time of ManipTrans, DexMachina or CHORD in Tab. 2. The reward-gated decay of the virtual object controllers of DexMachina does not start within its budget. These controllers thus decay linearly to zero over the first two thirds of its training, and we score it after they reach zero. Its objects then mostly stay within the 10 cm of SPSR but rarely within the 3 cm of MP-SR. Our floating hand is driven at the wrist by six virtual joints, three prismatic and three revolute. Scoring. Unlike acceptance, every rollout runs to the end of the clip with object-tracking termination off, and we score the final checkpoint. Each step of method is scored against the original object motion at the time that step maps to, so that method that slows the motion down is compared with the same demonstration. SP-SR requires mean object error within 10 cm and 0.5 rad, the rule of SPIDER, and MPSR requires the object criteria of ManipTrans, within 3 cm and 30. As SPIDER and EgoEngine output one trajectory per run, Tab. S5 also scores the same evaluations by the mean over rollouts, without rerun. Scored this way, the arm-mounted policies with = 64 still score above every prior method in every metric. E.3. FlashDexRetarget and our recipe FlashDexRetarget [20] gives each hand its own actor and critic, while our two actors share one critic trunk with value head per hand. In its released code, the wrist adds bounded residual to the reference as ours does, while the finger joints take absolute targets within their limits instead of shifting the reference angles. It also observes ten future reference frames and object point clouds, rewards distances instead of matching contact between hand and object points, and trains off-policy with FlashSAC, replay buffer of 50M transitions and critic of width 1,024. Our floating-hand policy trains for about 210M environment steps against FlashDexRetargets 500M. Of its 16-fold cost per clip in Tab. 2, factor of 2.4 thus comes from more steps and factor of 6.7 from higher cost per step. 20 OT3D OakInk
